claims.C-01: The rules engine plays 530–555 complete random games per second on one CPU core of a 2015 laptop (Intel Core i5-5350U).
claims.C-02: The engine's legal moves were cross-checked against two independent Brass: Birmingham implementations.
claims.C-03: The default neural network has 390,342 parameters and passes messages between cities, links and players.
claims.C-04: 1,586 self-play training games on the main line so far.
claims.C-05: Latest main checkpoint: update 793. Working model: BC 788.
claims.C-06: 1,058 playable model versions are kept, each with its exact identity and lineage.
claims.C-08: One training variant won 32 of 32 games against three rule-based Greedy players.
claims.C-09: Highest recorded score by an AI player: 124 victory points (ppo-843-new, an experiment branch from the main line, evaluation game against three AI players). Previous record: 108 (ppo-660).
claims.C-10: Training, evaluation and live games are recorded automatically and can be replayed move by move.
claims.C-11: A typical game has about 172 decisions with about 72 legal options each (measured on two training games: 343 decisions, 24,540 legal candidates).
claims.C-12: 772 training games in one 11 h 19 min free Kaggle CPU session.
claims.C-13: One two-game training update takes 52.33 s on CPU (median).
claims.C-14: Trained with no paid compute: a consumer laptop and free Kaggle CPU sessions.
claims.C-15: Brass: Birmingham was listed by Guinness World Records as the highest-rated game on BoardGameGeek (18 March 2025, weighted average 8.404).
claims.C-16: Mean AI seat score rose from 7.7 VP (updates 0–19, 2,570 seat scores, mostly the untrained model) to 63.5 VP (updates 820–839, 185 seat scores), across 13,414 recorded AI seat scores.
claims.C-17: Pass fell from 29.9% of main actions (updates 0–39) to 1.1% (updates 800–839).
